title: How the web works
summary: Every website begins with a conversation between a browser and a server. You will follow one request from a typed URL to pixels on a screen.
concept: A URL identifies a resource. DNS finds the server, HTTPS carries the request, and the server returns files such as HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The browser parses those files and paints the page.
code:
Browser  →  HTTPS request  →  Web server
Browser  ←  HTML + CSS + JS  ←  Web server
challenge: Open the Network panel on any website and identify its first document request.

title: Your first HTML document
summary: HTML gives content meaning. Build a valid document and learn what the browser does with each element.
concept: A page has one document type, an html root, metadata inside head, and visible content inside body. Semantic tags describe purpose rather than appearance.
code:
Hello, web!

I built this with HTML.
challenge: Create a page with one heading, two paragraphs and a link to a site you use often.

title: Semantic & accessible HTML
summary: Good structure helps people, browsers and search engines understand your page.
concept: Use landmarks such as header, nav, main and footer. Pair every form input with a label, keep headings in order, and write useful alternative text for meaningful images.
code:
Learning in public

Small projects create visible progress.
challenge: Replace the generic div elements in a sample page with at least four semantic elements.

title: CSS foundations
summary: Use selectors, properties and values to control how HTML looks and responds.
concept: The cascade combines browser defaults, inherited values, selector specificity and source order. Start with simple class selectors and let layout rules do most of the work.
challenge: Create a reusable card class with spacing, a border, rounded corners and a subtle shadow.

title: Layouts with Flexbox & Grid
summary: Stop positioning elements by guesswork. Use two layout systems designed for interfaces.
concept: Flexbox arranges items along one main axis and is ideal for nav bars and rows. Grid controls rows and columns together and is ideal for page sections and card collections.
challenge: Build a card grid that shows one column on small screens and three when space allows.

title: Responsive design
summary: Make one interface feel intentional on phones, tablets and large screens.
concept: Start with a fluid mobile layout, use flexible units, and add a breakpoint only when the content needs it. Test narrow widths and keyboard zoom—not just popular device presets.
challenge: Audit your project at 320px, 768px and 1280px. Fix every horizontal scrollbar.

title: Ship your portfolio
summary: Combine the course skills, check quality and put your work online.
concept: A useful launch checklist covers content, responsive layout, keyboard navigation, page metadata, image sizes and broken links. Shipping creates feedback you cannot get from a local file.
code:
git add .
git commit -m "ship portfolio v1"
git push origin main
challenge: Publish your portfolio and ask one person to complete a task on it without your help.

title: What computers actually do
summary: Behind every app, a computer repeatedly accepts input, stores data, transforms it and produces output.
concept: Hardware performs a small vocabulary of operations extremely quickly. Software creates useful abstractions by combining those operations into instructions, functions and systems.
code:
input → store → process → output
             ↖ repeat ↙
challenge: Choose a familiar app and list its inputs, stored data, processing steps and outputs.

title: Bits, bytes & data
summary: Text, photos and sound all become patterns of two states before a computer can store them.
concept: A bit is 0 or 1. Eight bits form a byte. Interpretation gives a bit pattern meaning: the same bits can represent a number, a character or part of a pixel depending on the format.
code:
13 in decimal = 1101 in binary
8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13
challenge: Convert the decimal numbers 7, 18 and 42 to binary using place values.

title: Logic & algorithms
summary: Turn an unclear goal into a finite sequence of unambiguous steps.
concept: An algorithm has defined inputs, ordered operations and an expected output. Conditions choose a path; loops repeat work; functions name and reuse a process.
challenge: Write pseudocode that finds the smallest price in a shopping basket.

title: Data structures
summary: The way data is organized changes which operations are easy, fast or expensive.
concept: Arrays provide ordered indexed access, stacks use last-in-first-out, queues use first-in-first-out, and maps connect unique keys to values. Pick the structure that matches the operations you perform most.
code:
stack.push(task)
latest = stack.pop()

profileById.set(user.id, user)
challenge: For browser history, a support queue and a phone book, choose a data structure and explain why.

title: Memory, programs & processes
summary: Understand what changes when a program on disk becomes a running process.
concept: The operating system gives each process resources and a protected address space. The stack tracks active function calls; the heap stores dynamically allocated data that can outlive one call.
code:
program file → operating system loads it → running process
                                  ↳ memory + CPU time
challenge: Open your system monitor, find three processes and compare their memory use.

title: Networks & the internet
summary: Learn how independently owned networks cooperate to move information around the world.
concept: Packets carry small pieces of data. IP handles addressing and routing, TCP provides ordered delivery, and application protocols such as HTTP define the messages programs exchange.
code:
application: HTTP
transport:   TCP
network:     IP
link:        Wi‑Fi / Ethernet
challenge: Run a traceroute to a public website and note how many network hops appear.

title: Values & variables
summary: Programs become useful when they can remember information and transform it.
concept: Use const by default and let when a binding must change. JavaScript values include strings, numbers, booleans, null, undefined, objects and functions.
challenge: Create variables for a course title, total lessons and completed lessons, then calculate the percentage.

title: Conditions & loops
summary: Control which instructions run and how often they repeat.
concept: Conditions branch on boolean expressions. for...of reads naturally when you need every value in a collection; array methods can express transformations with less manual state.
challenge: Loop through five lesson scores and count how many are 70 or higher.

title: Functions & scope
summary: Package behavior into small, named units that are easier to reuse and test.
concept: Parameters are a function's inputs and return values are its outputs. Scope controls where names are visible. Prefer functions that do one clear job and return data instead of changing distant state.
challenge: Write and call a function that converts minutes into a friendly hours-and-minutes label.

title: Arrays & objects
summary: Model lists and structured records, then combine them to represent real application data.
concept: Arrays preserve order. Objects group related values by key. Methods such as map, filter and find produce concise data pipelines without manually managing indexes.
challenge: From an array of course objects, return the titles of beginner courses only.

title: The DOM & events
summary: Read the page as data, respond to people and update only what changed.
concept: The DOM is the browser's object representation of HTML. Query stable selectors, listen for events, update accessible state and keep business logic separate from rendering code.
challenge: Add a button that toggles a card between incomplete and complete states.

title: Async JavaScript & APIs
summary: Request data without freezing the page and handle every outcome clearly.
concept: Promises represent future results. await makes promise-based code easier to read. A resilient request handles loading, success, empty and error states rather than assuming the network always works.
challenge: Fetch a public JSON endpoint and render both a loading message and an error message.

title: Build & ship the task planner
summary: Bring state, events, storage and an API together in one maintainable project.
concept: Plan data first, render from that data, route every interaction through a small set of update functions, and persist only the state needed after refresh.
challenge: Ship the planner with add, complete, filter and persistence features.

title: The React mental model
summary: React lets you describe what the interface should look like for the current data.
concept: A component is a function of props and state. Rendering calculates a UI description; committing applies the necessary changes to the browser. Keep rendering pure and put side effects in event handlers or effects.
challenge: Break a dashboard screenshot into a named component tree.

title: Props & composition
summary: Create flexible components by passing data and nesting content rather than adding endless options.
concept: Props flow down from parent to child. Composition through children or focused slots lets callers control content while the component owns layout and behavior.
challenge: Create one Card component and use it for a metric, a chart and an empty state.

title: State & events
summary: Represent the smallest changing facts and derive everything else during render.
concept: State belongs in the closest common owner of every component that needs it. Avoid duplicate state: if a value can be calculated from props or existing state, calculate it.
challenge: Build a searchable list with one source of truth for the query.

title: Forms & validation
summary: Turn user input into clear, accessible and trustworthy interactions.
concept: Validate at useful moments, connect errors to fields, preserve input after failure and never rely on client validation for security. Server validation remains the final authority.
challenge: Build a profile form with inline errors and a visible successful-save state.

title: Data fetching states
summary: Design the full lifecycle of remote data, not only the successful screenshot.
concept: A data view needs loading, error, empty, stale and success states. Cancel obsolete requests and avoid waterfalls by loading independent resources together.
code:
const [data, setData] = useState(null);
const [status, setStatus] = useState("loading");
challenge: Create a data panel that can display a skeleton, retry error, empty state and results.

title: Routing & app architecture
summary: Give every major screen a stable URL and organize code around product features.
concept: Routes should match user concepts. Keep feature-specific components close to their route, share truly generic UI, and draw a clear boundary between server data and interactive client state.
code:
app/
  dashboard/page.tsx
  courses/[slug]/page.tsx
components/
lib/
challenge: Design routes and folders for an online learning dashboard with course and lesson pages.

title: Ship the analytics dashboard
summary: Polish performance, accessibility and edge cases before you call the build complete.
concept: Measure before optimizing. Check keyboard flow, semantic landmarks, loading performance, error recovery and small screens. Then document the decisions another developer needs to continue.
code:
npm run build
# fix every error before deployment
challenge: Deploy the dashboard and complete a keyboard-only quality audit.

title: Native apps vs the web
summary: Understand what React Native shares with React and what changes on iOS and Android.
concept: React Native uses React's component model but renders native views rather than HTML. There is no browser DOM, CSS differs, and platform conventions matter to how an app feels.
challenge: List three browser APIs a web app may use that a native app cannot assume exist.

title: Layouts & styling
summary: Create adaptable mobile layouts with Flexbox, safe areas and platform-aware spacing.
concept: React Native defaults to a vertical flex direction. Use StyleSheet for named styles, respect safe areas and test dynamic text sizes instead of designing around one simulator.
challenge: Build a habit card that remains readable with the device font size increased.

title: Navigation patterns
summary: Connect screens using navigation that matches platform expectations.
concept: Stacks model drill-down flows, tabs switch top-level areas and modals isolate focused tasks. Keep route parameters small and load full records from shared state.
code: <Stack.Screen name="HabitDetail" component={HabitDetail} />
challenge: Sketch a route map for a habit app with Today, Progress, Settings and Habit Detail screens.

title: State & device storage
summary: Keep useful data between sessions without making the interface wait unnecessarily.
concept: Store small non-sensitive preferences locally, use a secure store for secrets, and treat serialization as an explicit boundary. Show a stable loading screen while restoring initial state.
code: await AsyncStorage.setItem("habits", JSON.stringify(habits));
challenge: Persist a list of habits and safely recover if the stored JSON is invalid.

title: Gestures, feedback & polish
summary: Make taps, transitions and system feedback feel immediate and intentional.
concept: Touch targets need enough space, destructive actions need confirmation or undo, and haptics should reinforce—not replace—visual information. Keep animation tied to meaning.
code:
<Pressable hitSlop={8} accessibilityRole="button">
  <Text>Mark complete</Text>
</Pressable>
challenge: Audit every control in your app for touch size, label and pressed feedback.

title: Test & release
summary: Move from a working simulator build to an app other people can install confidently.
concept: Test real devices, slow networks, offline launches, denied permissions and interrupted flows. Prepare icons, screenshots, privacy details and versioned builds before store review.
code:
npx expo-doctor
npx eas build --platform all
challenge: Create a release checklist and run your core flow on one physical device.

title: Node.js & the server runtime
summary: Use JavaScript outside the browser and understand the event-driven runtime behind it.
concept: Node.js runs JavaScript with operating-system APIs for files, processes and networking. Its event loop is effective for many concurrent I/O tasks when code avoids blocking work.
challenge: Create a server with a /health endpoint that returns JSON.

title: HTTP & RESTful routes
summary: Design resource-based routes with meaningful methods, statuses and response shapes.
concept: GET reads, POST creates, PATCH changes and DELETE removes. Status codes communicate the result. Consistent errors help every client recover predictably.
code:
GET    /api/courses
POST   /api/courses
GET    /api/courses/:id
PATCH  /api/courses/:id
challenge: Design the routes and response statuses for enrollment and lesson completion.

title: Validation & error handling
summary: Treat all external input as untrusted and turn failures into useful responses.
concept: Validate shape, type, range and permissions at the server boundary. Keep internal error detail out of public responses, but log enough context to investigate.
challenge: Add validation for an account payload with name, email and weekly goal.

title: Database modeling
summary: Turn product rules into tables, relationships, constraints and useful indexes.
concept: Give each entity a stable key, normalize facts that update independently and enforce rules with constraints. Add indexes for frequent lookup paths, not every column.
code:
users 1 ─── * enrollments * ─── 1 courses
users 1 ─── * lesson_progress * ─── 1 lessons
challenge: Model users, courses, lessons, purchases and progress with keys and relationships.

title: Authentication & permissions
summary: Know who is making a request, then verify what that person is allowed to do.
concept: Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks permission for the exact resource and action. Hash passwords with a dedicated slow algorithm and keep session cookies httpOnly and secure.
challenge: Write an authorization matrix for learners, instructors and administrators.

title: Test & deploy the API
summary: Prove important behavior automatically and prepare the service for real traffic.
concept: Test outcomes at the public boundary: status, response and database effect. Use environment variables for secrets, health checks for operations and structured logs for investigation.
challenge: Write integration tests for successful completion, locked course access and suspended accounts.

title: Big-O without the fear
summary: Big-O is just a way of saying how work grows when the input doubles. It is the vocabulary for every performance conversation you will ever have.
concept: Count the steps an algorithm takes as the input grows. A loop over n items is O(n); a loop inside a loop is O(n²); halving the problem each pass is O(log n). Constants and small terms are dropped because they stop mattering at scale.
challenge: Take two functions you wrote last week and label each one with its Big-O. Write the number of steps for inputs of 10 and 1,000.

title: Arrays, strings and two pointers
summary: Arrays are contiguous memory with instant indexed reads, which makes them the right home for ordered data — and the right problem for two-pointer tricks.
concept: Reading `list[i]` costs the same whatever `i` is, but inserting at the front shifts everything. Two pointers walk a sorted array from both ends so a nested loop collapses into a single pass.
challenge: Reverse a string in place with two pointers instead of a library call, then say why the loop runs n/2 times.

title: Maps and sets: looking things up in one step
summary: A hash map turns 'search the list' into 'ask the map'. Most 'slow' code becomes fast the moment the inner loop is replaced with a lookup.
concept: A hash function turns a key into a position, so insert, find and delete average O(1). Sets are maps without values — perfect for 'have I seen this before?'.
challenge: Count how many times each word appears in a paragraph with one pass and one Map. Then explain what changed versus sorting first.

title: Sorting and searching
summary: Sorting is the move that makes everything else cheaper: searching, de-duplicating, merging and grouping all get simpler on ordered data.
concept: Binary search halves the search space each step, so a million sorted items take about twenty comparisons. Sorting first costs O(n log n) and then each search is O(log n) — a bargain when you search many times.
challenge: Search a sorted list of a million numbers for a missing value and count the comparisons in your head before you run it.

title: Recursion and memoization
summary: Recursion solves a problem by solving a smaller copy of itself. Memoization makes recursive solutions fast by never solving the same smaller problem twice.
concept: Naive Fibonacci recomputes the same values exponentially many times — O(2ⁿ). Caching each result the first time it is computed drops the whole tree to O(n).
challenge: Write a recursive coin-change counter, then add a cache and measure both versions on the same input.

title: Trees, graphs and traversal
summary: A tree is a hierarchy (files, comments, decisions). A graph is anything connected to anything (friends, routes, dependencies). Both are searched the same two ways.
concept: Depth-first search follows one branch to the end, which suits small graphs and recursion. Breadth-first search explores level by level, which is how you find the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
challenge: Model a small map as an object of neighbours and find the shortest route between two stops with BFS.

title: Tables, rows and keys
summary: A database is a set of tables where every row is one thing and every column is one fact about it. Keys are what keep rows from lying about each other.
concept: A primary key identifies a row forever. A foreign key says 'this value must exist in that table', which lets the database refuse inconsistent data instead of storing it.
challenge: Model a small library: books, members and loans. Every loan must point at a real member and a real book.

title: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY
summary: Most questions you have about data are three clauses: which table, which rows, in what order.
concept: Select only the columns you need, filter with WHERE, sort with ORDER BY and page with LIMIT. NULL is not equal to anything — it needs `IS NULL`.
code:
select name, email
  from students
 where email is not null
   and name ilike 'a%'
 order by name asc
 limit 20;
challenge: Write a query that returns the five most recently enrolled students and their course.

title: Joins: asking across tables
summary: Data lives in separate tables so it is stored once. Joins are how you put the story back together for one question.
concept: An INNER JOIN keeps rows that match on both sides. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table even when nothing matches — which is how you find students with no enrolments (the `IS NULL` filter).
code:
select s.name, c.title, e.grade
  from enrolments e
  join students s on s.id = e.student_id
  join courses  c on c.id = e.course_id
 order by s.name;

-- Everyone who has never enrolled:
select s.name
  from students s
  left join enrolments e on e.student_id = s.id
 where e.id is null;
challenge: List every course with how many students are enrolled in it, including the courses with none.

title: Insert, update and delete safely
summary: Writes are where mistakes become permanent, so they should be narrow: touch the rows you mean and nothing else.
concept: The dangerous part of UPDATE and DELETE is the WHERE clause — forget it and you rewrite the whole table. `RETURNING` shows exactly what changed, so you never have to guess.
challenge: Insert a student and their first enrolment in one transaction, then update the grade and print the changed row.

title: Indexes and EXPLAIN
summary: An index is a sorted shortcut the database keeps so it does not read the whole table for one lookup. EXPLAIN shows you whether it was used.
concept: Indexes cost storage and slow down writes, so you add them for the queries you actually run — filters, joins and sorts. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` is the honest measure: it runs the query and reports the real time.
challenge: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after adding an index on a column you filter by, and compare the row counts.

title: Transactions and constraints
summary: A transaction makes several statements one all-or-nothing unit, which is what keeps money, stock and enrolments correct when two people act at once.
concept: BEGIN opens it, COMMIT makes it real, ROLLBACK undoes it. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the rows you are about to change so a second request waits instead of double-spending.
challenge: Book the last seat of a class from two sessions at the same time. Confirm one succeeds and the other waits, then explain why.

title: Branches, commits and pull requests
summary: Version control is a safety net and a conversation at the same time: small commits explain what changed, and a pull request explains why.
concept: A branch is a moving label on a commit. Commit in small, complete steps with a message that finishes the sentence 'this change will…'. Then open a pull request so the change can be read before it reaches main.
code:
git switch -c add-gradebook
git add src/gradebook.ts
git commit -m "Add a gradebook that averages scores per student"
git push -u origin add-gradebook
gh pr create --fill
challenge: Take a change you already made, split it into two commits that each do one thing, and write both messages.

title: Code review that helps
summary: Review is about the code, not the person. A good review catches real problems, shares context and leaves the author able to move faster.
concept: Review for correctness first, then clarity, then style — and say why. Approve small changes quickly; ask questions rather than issuing commands, and always explain the risk you are pointing at.
code:
> "This works, but `users.find()` inside the loop makes it O(n²).
> Could we build a Map keyed by id first? That would also
> make the intent clearer."
challenge: Review a pull request you wrote last month. Leave three comments: one bug, one clarity, one praise.

title: Naming and structure that survives
summary: Code is read far more often than it is written. Good names and small functions are what make a change safe six months later.
concept: A name should say what a thing is or does, not what type it is. Keep functions at one level of abstraction, delete dead code instead of commenting it, and let the shape of the data explain the flow.
challenge: Rename the worst three names in a file you own, without changing behaviour, and check the diff reads better.

title: Tests that earn their keep
summary: A test is a promise about behaviour. The good ones describe real rules, fail for exactly one reason and run in milliseconds.
concept: Arrange, act, assert. Test the interesting cases: empty input, the boundary, the error path. If a test needs a database, an API and a fake clock, that is usually the design asking to be split.
challenge: Write three tests for a function you already shipped: a normal case, a boundary and a failure.

title: A pipeline on every push
summary: Continuous integration is a robot that runs the boring checks for you: install, typecheck, test, build. It turns 'it worked on my machine' into a fact.
concept: Keep the pipeline fast and honest — the same commands a developer runs locally. Fail loudly, and never merge a red build: a pipeline people ignore is worse than none.
code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test
challenge: Add a workflow to one of your repositories that runs typecheck and tests, and make it fail on purpose once to see the red mark.

title: Issues, scope and shipping small
summary: Engineering is mostly deciding what not to build yet. Small, shippable increments keep quality high and feedback quick.
concept: Write an issue as the user problem and the smallest acceptable change. Slice work so each slice is releasable. Estimate by comparing to work you have already done, not by guessing hours.
code:
## Problem
Students cannot tell which lesson is a free preview.

## Smallest acceptable change
Show a "Free preview" chip in the course lesson list.

## Not in this slice
Filtering, badges on cards, analytics.
challenge: Take your current project and cut it into three releases, each of which a real user could use.

title: Clients, APIs and contracts
summary: An API is a promise: what you can ask for, what you will get back, and what happens when it goes wrong. Everything else in the system hangs off that promise.
concept: Keep resources nouns and verbs in HTTP methods. Return the same shape for the same kind of error, version the contract when it must change, and make writes idempotent so a retry cannot double-charge.
challenge: Write the API contract for booking a seat, including the two failure responses a client must handle.

title: Choosing where data lives
summary: The data model decides how the system behaves under load. Schemas, read patterns and consistency all follow from what the product must never get wrong.
concept: Relational databases give you joins and transactions; key-value stores give you speed and simple scale; search engines give you text. Most products want one relational core plus a derived read model for the query that is too slow.
code:
bookings (id, event_id, seat_id, state, held_until)
  unique (event_id, seat_id) where state <> 'cancelled'

-- Derived read model, rebuilt from bookings:
seat_availability (event_id, seat_id, available boolean)
challenge: Model seats and bookings so that a seat can never be sold twice, even with two simultaneous buyers.

title: Caches, queues and eventual work
summary: A cache answers a question faster than the source of truth. A queue moves work out of the request so a slow job cannot slow the user down.
concept: Cache what is read often and changes rarely, and always have an expiry. Put email, image processing and reports on a queue with retries — then design the retry so a duplicate job is harmless.
challenge: List every slow or unreliable step in your project and mark each one: cache it, queue it, or leave it inline.

title: Designing for failure
summary: Everything fails: disks, networks, third parties, your own deploy. Reliability is deciding what should happen when it does.
concept: Use timeouts everywhere, retry only idempotent work, and add a circuit breaker so one slow dependency cannot consume every request. Degrade instead of collapsing — a cached page beats a 500.
challenge: Take your last outage or bug and write the three changes that would have contained it.

title: Authentication, authorisation and the obvious holes
summary: Security is mostly boring discipline: trust the server, check every request, store less, and never let the browser decide what a user may do.
concept: Authenticate once, authorise every request. Hash passwords with a slow algorithm, keep secrets out of the client, validate input at the boundary and check ownership before returning anything.
challenge: Pick a route in your app and list who can call it, what they must prove, and what the server checks before answering.

title: Trade-offs, and writing them down
summary: Every design decision buys something and pays for it elsewhere. An architecture decision record is how the next engineer learns why.
concept: An ADR is short: context, decision, consequences. Write the alternatives you rejected and the conditions under which you would revisit — that is what turns an opinion into engineering.
code:
# ADR 3: Hold seats with a short-lived reservation

Context   Two buyers can pick the same seat at once.
Decision  Create a booking row with state 'held' for 10 minutes.
Alternatives  In-memory lock (lost on deploy); queue all bookings (slower UX).
Consequences  Need a sweeper to expire holds; a crash cannot oversell.
Revisit if  Holds exceed 20% of traffic.
challenge: Write one ADR for a decision you have already made. Include the option you rejected and why.

title: Environments and config
summary: The same code should run everywhere; only the configuration differs. Everything else is how a bug reaches production.
concept: Keep secrets in the environment, never in the repo. Fail fast at boot when a required variable is missing, and give each environment its own database — sharing one is how a test wipes real data.
challenge: List every environment variable your app reads, mark which are secret, and make the app refuse to start without the required ones.

title: Containers you can trust
summary: A container packages your app and its runtime so the build is the same on your laptop, in CI and in production.
concept: Use a small base image, install dependencies from the lockfile, copy source last so layers cache, and run as a non-root user. One process per container; state belongs in a volume or a database.
code:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
USER node
ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
challenge: Write a Dockerfile for one of your projects and check the image builds twice in a row with the cache hit.

title: Deploy and rollback
summary: Deployment should be one command that either finishes or leaves the previous version running. Rolling back should be one more.
concept: Build an immutable artifact, deploy it, run a smoke test against the real URL and only then switch traffic. Keep the previous release so rollback is a pointer change, not a rebuild.
code:
npm ci && npm run build
ssh deploy@host 'ln -sfn releases/$(date +%s) current && systemctl reload app'
curl -fsS https://app.example.com/api/health || ./rollback.sh
challenge: Add a health check to your app and make your deploy script refuse to finish unless it returns healthy.

title: Monitoring that wakes you, logs that explain
summary: Metrics tell you something is wrong; logs tell you why. You need both, and you need them before the incident.
concept: Track the four signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Log structured events with a request id, never log secrets or full personal data, and alert on symptoms users feel rather than on CPU.
challenge: Add one structured log line and one timing metric to a route you care about, then decide the threshold that should page you.

title: Backups and schema changes
summary: Data outlives code. Migrations must be safe to run while the old version is still serving traffic, and backups are only real once you have restored one.
concept: Add columns as nullable, backfill, then enforce — never rename and rewrite in one step. Test the restore, not the backup, and write down how long recovery takes.
challenge: Write the migration order for renaming a column with zero downtime, then restore a backup into a scratch database.

title: Incidents and blameless reviews
summary: Every outage is a lesson with a timestamp. The goal of a review is a system that cannot fail the same way, not a person to blame.
concept: During an incident: stop the bleeding (roll back), then investigate. Afterwards write the timeline from data, name the contributing causes honestly and turn each one into an issue with an owner.
code:
12:04  Deploy 41 ships; error rate 0.2% -> 14%
12:06  Rollback to 40; errors return to baseline
12:20  Root cause: migration added NOT NULL before backfill
Action: migrations must be additive-only in one release (owner: NA)
challenge: Write the timeline of the last bug that hit production, from the deploy to the fix, and turn it into three actions.

title: What vibe coding actually is
summary: Vibe coding is writing software by describing what you want and reviewing what comes back. It is fast because the AI types; it works because you decide.
concept: The loop is: describe one thing, run it, read the diff, keep or reject, then repeat. Small steps keep the code reviewable — a giant prompt produces a giant change nobody can check.
code:
1. Describe ONE change, with the file and the expected behaviour
2. Let the AI write it
3. Run it and look at the result
4. Read the diff: does it do exactly this, and nothing more?
5. Commit. Then describe the next thing.
challenge: Write the description of a single small feature you want, as if briefing a developer. Then get the AI to build only that.

title: Prompts that produce working code
summary: A good prompt is a tiny spec: the goal, the constraints, the shape of the data and how you will know it works.
concept: Name the stack and the file, give the inputs and outputs, state what must not change, and ask for the smallest diff. When the answer is wrong, add the missing constraint instead of rewriting the whole prompt.
code:
Goal: a route that lists a student's purchases.
Stack: Next.js App Router, TypeScript, no new dependencies.
Input: the signed-in user.
Output: { purchases: [{ kind, refId, amount, at }] }.
Must not: touch the database schema or add a package.
Done when: it typechecks and returns [] for a new account.
challenge: Take a prompt you already sent and rewrite it with goal, constraints, data shape and done-when.

title: Reading code you did not write
summary: The skill that separates a vibe coder from a passenger is reading: find the data, follow the flow, spot the edge case the AI forgot.
concept: Read the diff, not the chat. Ask where the data comes from, what happens on empty and on error, and what the code assumes about the caller. If you cannot explain a line, that is the line to change.
challenge: Ask the AI for a function, then write down every assumption it made. Fix the one that would break first.

title: Build a working page in an hour
summary: One page, real data, styled and deployed. The point is the loop, not the size of the project.
concept: Start from a template that already runs, keep state in one place, and let the AI do the styling passes after the behaviour works. Deploy early — a URL changes how you judge your own work.
challenge: Build and deploy a one-page app today: an input, a list, and a button that adds to it.

title: Iterating and debugging with AI
summary: When something breaks, the AI needs evidence, not adjectives. Paste the error, the input and what you expected.
concept: Reproduce first, then give the smallest failing case. Ask for one hypothesis at a time, and make it explain the cause before it writes the fix — otherwise you get a patch over a bug.
code:
It fails on this exact input:
  join([], "-")  ->  expected "", got undefined

The error: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

Explain the cause before changing anything, then give me the smallest fix.
challenge: Take a real bug, write the smallest failing case, and ask for the cause before the fix. Note what the first fix got wrong.

title: Polish, publish, and keep it alive
summary: Shipping is a checklist, not a feeling: empty states, error messages, a title, a favicon, and a way to see when it breaks.
concept: Handle the states a demo never shows — loading, empty and error. Write a README with how to run it, add a health check, and tag the commit you deployed so you can go back.
code:
Loading → skeletons, not a spinner forever
Empty   → "No projects yet. Create your first one."
Error   → "That did not save. Try again." + a retry button
README  → what it is, how to run it, how it deploys
challenge: Go through your app and add the empty and error states for every list and form.

title: Calling a model from your server
summary: The model call belongs on the server, behind your own API, where the key lives and where you can log, limit and cache it.
concept: Send a system prompt, the message history and a token limit. Always set a timeout, always handle a refusal or an empty answer, and never put the provider key in the browser.
challenge: Add a server route that asks a model one question and returns its answer. Log the tokens used.

title: The prompt is product surface
summary: A prompt is not a string in a file — it is behaviour your users feel. Treat it like code: versioned, reviewed and tested.
concept: Put the instructions, the tone and the refusal rule in one place. Say what to do when it does not know, keep the output shape stable, and change it with a test that shows the difference.
code:
You are the support assistant for codemasterghana.
Answer in at most three sentences, in plain English.
Use ONLY the notes below. If the notes do not contain the
answer, reply exactly: "I will pass this to a human."

Notes:
{{retrieved}}
challenge: Write your system prompt with an explicit refusal rule, then try three questions it should refuse.

title: Your own data: retrieval (RAG)
summary: Models do not know your product. Retrieval finds the few paragraphs that matter and puts them in the prompt, so answers are grounded in your documents.
concept: Split documents into overlapping chunks, embed them, store the vectors, then search for the closest chunks to the question and pass those as context. Return citations so the user can check.
challenge: Index five of your own pages and ask a question whose answer appears in only one of them.

title: Tools and agents
summary: An agent is a model that can call your functions: look up an order, create a ticket, send a receipt. The power and the risk are the same thing.
concept: Expose narrow, well-named tools with validated arguments. The model proposes a call; your code decides whether to run it — permissions, limits and confirmations stay on your side.
challenge: Give your assistant one read-only tool and one write tool. Write down who is allowed to trigger the write.

title: Evals, latency and cost
summary: You cannot improve what you do not measure. A small set of real questions, scored automatically, is worth more than any demo.
concept: Keep a test set of questions with expected answers or rubrics, run it on every prompt change, and record tokens, latency and failures. Cap the spend per user and per day.
challenge: Build a five-question suite for your assistant and record the pass rate, average latency and tokens per answer.

title: Safety, privacy and shipping
summary: Shipping AI means deciding what it may never see, say or do — and making those decisions in code, not in the prompt alone.
concept: Sent prompts and outputs are data: keep personal details out, tell users they are talking to an AI, keep a human path for anything that matters, and log enough to investigate without storing more than you need.
code:
Rules the code enforces, not just the prompt:
- strip emails, phones and card numbers before the call
- refuse medical, legal and financial advice
- "Talk to a human" button on every answer
- keep a 30-day log of prompts and citations, no raw PII
challenge: Write your assistant's data rules: what it may receive, what it must never store, and how a user reaches a human.
